name: progressive-web-app
context: A web application that must start reliably on slow or absent connections, serve the content the user last interacted with, and update itself in place. The architecture is a service worker that sits between the application and the network as middleware: it intercepts every request within its scope and acts as a proxy, even when the device is offline. Around that sit the app shell as a precached minimal UI, versioned caches whose lifecycle is tied to the worker's install/activate events, and background mechanisms that let work continue while the application is closed.
benefits: Repeat visits render instantly from cache instead of the network, which is where most perceived performance lives
Navigation requests resolve to a cached app shell, so an unvisited URL still produces a working interface instead of a browser error page
Cache strategies are chosen per resource — precache the shell, stale-while-revalidate assets, network-first data
The worker survives the application being closed and is restarted on a triggering event, enabling background sync and push
Installable and app-like delivery without an app store review or a user installing anything
tradeoffs: Two layers of caching exist — the HTTP cache and the Cache Storage API — and debugging 'why is this stale' requires understanding both
Version skew is inherent: the new worker installs in the background while the old one still serves, until every client is released or skipWaiting is called
In-memory state does not survive worker termination, so anything reused between runs must be persisted (typically IndexedDB)
The worker thread is killed when idle, which bounds background work and makes long tasks the job of Background Fetch
Adds weight and complexity to the client for applications that never work offline
use_cases: Content and commerce sites that must render on a flaky mobile connection
An application shell that loads instantly on repeat visits and shows content while data loads
Read-only or semi-offline experiences where caching media and tickets matters more than live data
Web applications that need push notifications and periodic content refresh without being open
Replacing a native install where store distribution is the main barrier
avoid_when: The application is cloud gaming or a crypto-asset wallet where full offline behaviour is not the goal
The content is highly personalised and uncacheable, making the shell the only useful artefact
Sensitive data must never be persisted on the device in a shared cache
A native or desktop client already provides the required offline and install behaviour
component_types: Service worker: network-proxy middleware on its own thread, scoped by the directory it is served from
Application shell: minimal HTML, CSS and JS (header, navigation, persistent chrome) precached at install time
Cache Storage: named, origin-scoped caches partitioned by version, populated during install and on route change
Fetch handler: per-resource strategy (cache-first, network-first, stale-while-revalidate, cache-only)
Lifecycle controller: install / waiting / activate transitions, old-cache cleanup, optional skipWaiting and clients.claim
Background mechanism: Background Sync, Background Fetch or Periodic Background Sync for work while the app is closed
anti_patterns: Precaching everything at install, wasting bandwidth and storage and serving unintended stale resources
Caching the HTML document permanently, so users never receive an updated application
Deleting the previous version's cache during install rather than during activate, breaking clients still on the old worker
Holding state in worker memory across events, which is discarded whenever the browser terminates the worker
Using Background Sync for long tasks, which the browser deliberately kills to limit IP exposure and battery use
design_principles: The worker is middleware, not a cache decorator — it owns the request path within its scope
Precache the shell; choose strategies per resource rather than one global policy
Version caches explicitly and delete old versions only on activate, once no client is using them
Offline is a capability, not a promise — degrade with your own messaging, never a browser error page
Worker state must be persisted, because the worker is terminated freely between events
best_practices: Use waitUntil around cache writes so the worker is not terminated mid-population
Serve navigation requests from the precached shell with navigateFallback so deep links work offline
Use clients.claim only when mid-session takeover is intended; it is what causes version-skew surprises
Require TLS for the Cache Storage API and keep cross-origin responses scoped to your origin
Use navigation preload so the fetch starts in parallel with worker activation instead of after it
